passage.title: Water for All
paras: Turn on a tap in Britain and clean water flows. For billions of people, it is not that simple.

According to the World Health Organization and UNICEF, which track water around the world through their Joint Monitoring Programme, 2.2 billion people did not have safely managed drinking water in 2022. That means water at home, available when needed and free from contamination. About three quarters of the world's people do have it, but more than a quarter still do not.

In 2010 the United Nations recognised clean water and sanitation as a human right. Yet in many places, fetching water is still a daily task, and in most households without water at home it is women and girls who carry it. Every hour spent walking to a well is an hour not spent in school.
Dirty water spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea, which are especially dangerous for young children. Safe water, clean toilets and handwashing save lives.

Water has always been precious. In Islam it is a trust from Allah: we are taught not to waste it, even when making wudu beside a flowing river. Using less at home and supporting charities that build wells are two ways to treat it as the gift it is.
